title: LLM decision trees for text classification without fine-tuning
description: Tree Prompting (EMNLP 2023) learns a text classifier whose internal nodes prompt a frozen language model and use its answers to select branches.
lead: In Tree Prompting: Efficient Task Adaptation without Fine-Tuning (EMNLP 2023), John X. Morris, Chandan Singh, Alexander M. Rush, Jianfeng Gao, and Yuntian Deng learn decision trees that classify text through prompted language-model calls. Each internal node asks the frozen model to judge the input; its answer selects the next branch, and the reached leaf returns a class. The learned prompts and branching structure form a reusable program for the task.

sections.title: What Tree Prompting introduced
paragraphs: The Tree Prompting preprint was released on 21 October 2023 and published at EMNLP 2023; John X. Morris and Chandan Singh contributed equally. A node combines a prompt, an LM call, and a rule mapping the output to a branch. A complete root-to-leaf path is the classifier’s execution trace for one input.

The tree is learned from labeled examples. Candidate prompts include sampled demonstrations, instructions and dynamically generated prompts. In the dynamic version, iPrompt generates candidates for the examples reaching a node, then split quality selects the prompt. Both the node questions and the tree’s branching structure are learned.

sections.title: From input text to node decisions to a class
paragraphs: Consider a worked support-classification example with input “I was charged twice; please refund the duplicate payment.” A first node asks whether the message requests a refund. Its yes branch reaches a node asking about a duplicate charge; that yes branch ends at a duplicate-billing leaf. The input is a message, the intermediate values are LM judgments, and the output is its category. This fixed example illustrates control flow; the paper learns its trees from data.

The program consists of conditions, branches and return values. A conventional condition tests a numerical threshold or an exact string. A prompt-based condition asks the LM to interpret the input under an instruction. The instruction defines the question; the LM supplies the decision for this particular input.

A path log distinguishes three failure types: the node asks an irrelevant question; the model answers a relevant question incorrectly; or the leaf assigns the wrong class after correct answers. Recording the actual path makes these failures distinguishable.

sections.title: What is learned, and what inference costs
paragraphs: Adaptation lives in the selected prompts and tree structure, without updating LM weights. Under one-call-per-node features, a path of depth D takes D LM calls, rather than evaluating every node. The code provides a scikit-learn-style classifier interface.

Keep fitting cost separate from prediction cost. Fitting searches candidate questions and measures their behavior on labeled inputs; serving evaluates the retained path. A large search budget therefore does not imply the same expense for every new prediction.

For an implementation, specify the label set, output parser, stopping rule and behavior on an invalid model answer. Measure accuracy together with average path length and token usage. Two trees with equal depth still differ in cost when their prompts include different numbers of demonstrations. Save the fitted prompts and tree with the model version: changing the LM changes the meaning of its executable conditions.

sections.title: Compare where the language model enters
paragraphs: Aug-Tree expands text features using an LLM during fitting, then deploys an interpretable tree without LM calls. GPTree builds LLM-powered trees and supports expert feedback on decision paths. ACT learns binary natural-language questions with impurity-based selection and TextGrad refinement.
These distinctions identify separate design choices: generating features, answering semantic questions, searching for better questions, and revising the resulting program.

sections.title: When a learned question tree is useful
paragraphs: Use this design when the task has a repeatable decision structure and labeled examples expose which distinctions matter. Intent routing, document classification and categorization all provide a natural setting for asking successive semantic questions. The tree stores task-specific structure outside the model weights.

Choose among example messages to follow their paths through a fixed tree. To train a classifier, use the original paper and code, fit on training examples, select tree size on validation data, and evaluate the saved tree on held-out examples.

sections.title: Run the original Tree Prompting notebook
paragraphs: The authors’ original notebook uses GPT-2 and Rotten Tomatoes examples to fit TreePromptClassifier, predict held-out labels, compare individual prompts, and draw the learned tree with plot_tree. Follow the repository installation instructions; this notebook downloads the model and dataset.

title: Energy-based text generation: whole-sequence scoring, resampling and diffusion
description: Residual Energy-Based Models for Text Generation (Yuntian Deng et al., ICLR 2020): globally normalized text generation, sample-and-score inference, and the connection to energy-based diffusion language models.
lead: A sequence-level energy model scores complete continuations, then uses those scores to change what a language model generates. Residual Energy-Based Models for Text Generation, by Yuntian Deng, Anton Bakhtin, Myle Ott, Arthur Szlam and Marc’Aurelio Ranzato (ICLR 2020), combines an autoregressive proposal with a learned whole-sequence energy in a globally normalized model. This formulation connects directly to energy-based diffusion language models, where the residual energy couples token predictions within a denoising step.
terms: token dependencies in diffusion language models

sections.title: How a whole-sequence energy generates text
paragraphs: Yuntian Deng, Anton Bakhtin, Myle Ott, Arthur Szlam and Marc’Aurelio Ranzato introduced the ICLR 2020 text-generation framework. Its arXiv version is dated 22 April 2020. A fixed autoregressive LM supplies candidate sequences; a bidirectional energy function scores them. The paper develops importance-weighted conditional generation and lower and upper log-probability bounds for perplexity evaluation.

The distribution is p(y | x) = q(y | x) exp(−E(x,y)) / Z(x). Here x is the context, y a complete continuation, q the base model, E the residual energy, and Z the normalizer over continuations. Lower energy increases probability relative to q. Noise-contrastive estimation trains the energy to distinguish real text from base-model samples.

sections.title: Why a discriminator can change a generator
paragraphs: The JMLR 2021 article, Residual Energy-Based Models for Text, develops the connection between distinguishing generated text and improving its distribution. Anton Bakhtin and Yuntian Deng contributed equally; Sam Gross, Myle Ott, Marc’Aurelio Ranzato and Arthur Szlam complete the author list. A discriminator supplies information about where a generator overproduces or underproduces text. A residual model turns that information into a probability correction.

The base model provides fluent proposals and their relative frequency. The energy changes their relative desirability after viewing the sequence. An energy of zero everywhere leaves the base distribution unchanged. Adding the same constant to every energy also leaves the normalized distribution unchanged, because the constant cancels between numerator and denominator.

Two algebraic checks apply regardless of the network that computes the scores: changing a shared energy offset leaves candidate-selection probabilities unchanged, while lowering one candidate’s energy increases its probability.

sections.title: Sample, score, then resample
paragraphs: Draw candidates from q, score each with E, and select with normalized weights proportional to exp(−E). This is importance resampling. Taking the highest-scoring candidate instead is reranking: it changes the selection rule. Both use a proposal-and-scoring pipeline, but define different output distributions.

For a worked example, assign three sampled candidates energies 0, log(2), and log(4). Their weights are 1, 1/2, and 1/4, giving selection probabilities 4/7, 2/7, and 1/7. Maximum-score selection always chooses the first candidate. Resampling preserves a distribution across the pool.

The base probability is already represented by drawing the pool from q. Multiplying each pool weight by q again changes the intended importance calculation. Likewise, a finite-pool normalizer is not an exact sum over all possible text. Increasing the number of proposals changes the approximation and the compute budget; changing the energy changes the target distribution.

sections.title: Where does the model represent dependencies between tokens?
paragraphs: The energy receives the complete candidate continuation. It can assign different scores to sequences that share a prefix but end differently, so the final selection depends on the words together. The base model proposes the text; the sequence-level energy changes the probability of the resulting continuation.

In diffusion generation, a denoiser proposes several unresolved tokens in parallel. EDLM applies the same base-times-energy construction to these proposed sequences, conditioned on the current noisy text. The sequence energy provides a joint correction for token dependencies. This is the concrete connection between residual EBM text generation and energy-based diffusion decoding.

sections.title: The direct connection to diffusion language models
paragraphs: Energy-Based Diffusion Language Models (EDLM), by Minkai Xu and colleagues, was released on 28 October 2024 and published at ICLR 2025. It multiplies a diffusion denoiser’s distribution by a sequence-level residual energy conditioned on the noisy sequence and timestep. This corrects dependencies missed by factorized token predictions within a denoising step.

EDLM uses either an autoregressive-model-derived energy or an energy trained by NCE, then generates through parallel importance sampling. It cites Deng et al. (2020) in its related work and explicitly uses that work in partition-function estimation. The relationship is mathematical and algorithmic: residual correction, contrastive training, resampling and likelihood estimation.

The 2020 model corrects an autoregressive proposal for text generation. EDLM corrects a denoising distribution inside an iterative diffusion process. The location of the correction changes; the base-times-energy construction connects them.

sections.title: Compare the base, energy and inference

Parallel proposals and resampling within denoising
Energy corrections for dependency and invariance

paragraphs: Wang and Ou’s neural TRF paper supplies an earlier residual formulation and NCE approach, credited explicitly in the 2020 paper. The 2020 contribution develops conditional text generation and likelihood evaluation around the residual model. Unified Energy (2026) extends the diffusion discussion by analyzing dependency and invariance errors and combining their energy corrections.

sections.title: Use the energy example to inspect the mechanism
paragraphs: Change the energy strength β over the three-outcome distribution in the example. At β = 0, the probabilities are the base distribution. Increasing β shifts mass toward lower-energy outcomes, while the base probabilities still affect the result.

For importance resampling from candidates already drawn from the base model, the pool weights are exp(−E(x)). The base-model factor is already accounted for by that sampling step. This distinction connects the normalized model to its practical sampling procedure.

sections.title: Run finite-pool energy resampling
paragraphs: Download the self-contained energy-resampling notebook or Python script. It computes the exact residual model on three outcomes, draws candidate pools from the base distribution, and selects entries using their energy weights.

It also sums over all possible pool-count configurations to compute the exact output distribution induced by a finite pool. This exposes the approximation error without Monte Carlo noise. Duplicate candidates retain their multiplicity, and selecting by minimum energy is shown separately from probabilistic resampling.
The code runs with Python 3.9+ and its standard library. Download all three examples and numerical checks.

title: CRFs for text generation: higher-order decoding, diffusion and candidate lattices
description: Yuntian Deng and Alexander M. Rush’s Cascaded Text Generation (NeurIPS 2020) and Sequence-to-Lattice (EMNLP Findings 2021): generate output tokens with structured inference and connect their dependencies to joint diffusion decoding.
lead: A conditional random field can generate text by making the output words its variables and decoding their joint sequence. Yuntian Deng and Alexander M. Rush developed higher-order CRF cascades in Cascaded Text Generation with Markov Transformers (NeurIPS 2020), then candidate-lattice generation with exact path search in Sequence-to-Lattice Models for Fast Translation (Findings of EMNLP 2021). These models connect parallel neural computation to dependent output decisions—the same coordination problem encountered when diffusion language models generate several tokens together.

sections.title: How does a CRF generate a sentence?
paragraphs: Let x be a source sentence and y₁, …, yₙ the target words to generate. Each yᵢ ranges over candidate output tokens. Potentials score combinations of neighboring words, conditioned on x; structured decoding chooses the output sequence. The predicted variables are the words of the translation itself.

Deng and Rush’s Cascaded Text Generation, first released on 1 June 2020, increases the Markov order across a cascade of CRFs. Higher-order factors score longer token spans, and a shared Markov Transformer computes their potentials. Their 2021 Sequence-to-Lattice model instead constructs a compact candidate lattice and scores first-order transitions before Viterbi path search. Both generate target sentences by modeling dependencies among output words.

sections.title: Why parallel predictions need a joint decision
paragraphs: Consider two valid continuations: “the dog runs” and “the dogs run.” Independent choices at each position also admit “the dog run.” Better representations help a network predict each marginal, but a product of marginals still cannot express that the noun and verb must agree. An explicit joint model assigns scores to combinations, making compatibility part of the output distribution and decoding procedure.

This separates two design choices: how expensive neural scores are computed, and how the final sequence is selected. Scores for many alternatives can be computed together, then combined by a small structured inference algorithm. Sun and colleagues’ Fast Structured Decoding for Sequence Models (NeurIPS 2019) combines non-autoregressive emissions with an approximate first-order CRF and dynamic transitions. Higher-order contexts, successive pruning, and candidate-lattice construction provide additional design choices.

sections.title: Higher-order CRFs: Cascaded Text Generation with Markov Transformers
paragraphs: Cascaded Text Generation introduces a sequence of CRFs with increasing Markov order. It begins with independent token scores, then adds dependencies over progressively longer spans. A single Markov Transformer supplies the potentials at every order through controlled context windows. Max-marginals score a span by the best complete sequence containing it; pruning retains promising spans before the next, more expressive stage.

The contribution combines higher-order output dependencies, shared neural parameterization, and parallel structured inference. This is distinct from the first-order dynamic CRF in Sun et al. Its parallel dynamic-programming formulation has logarithmic depth in sequence length for fixed retained width.

sections.title: How structured generation connects to joint diffusion decoding
paragraphs: Diffusion introduces a repeated version of the same coordination problem: several uncertain tokens are resolved during one denoising step. The connection to structured generation is a modeling principle: use a tractable joint distribution to couple those decisions while retaining parallel neural computation. A Markov order describes dependence across output positions; a diffusion timestep describes the progression from corrupted to recovered text. They are different axes.

CoDD, introduced in Breaking the Factorization Barrier in Diffusion Language Models (ICML 2026), combines factorized neural predictions with a probabilistic-circuit structural prior. Its experiments instantiate that prior with a hidden Markov model. The product supports joint inference without materializing a vocabulary-sized table for every possible token combination. This shares the structured-generation goal, while using latent-state structure and diffusion-conditioned inference rather than a cascade of increasing observed-token context orders.

DA-DLM (EMNLP 2026) makes the relationship to non-autoregressive translation explicit. It adapts directed-acyclic-graph modeling to iterative denoising: node groups correspond to output positions, and previously fixed tokens become anchors connected to unresolved candidates. Its graph changes as denoising proceeds. The earlier models apply structured output modeling to translation; DA-DLM places it inside diffusion denoising.

sections.title: Candidate lattices: Sequence-to-Lattice Models for Fast Translation
paragraphs: Sequence-to-Lattice replaces a deep decoder with candidate lookup, neural edge scoring, and path search. A statistical alignment model proposes a small vocabulary at each output position. A deep encoder and a shallow scoring head evaluate transitions between candidates in parallel. Viterbi then selects the highest-scoring complete path.

The paper specifies a first-order conditional Markov model with locally normalized transition probabilities. Viterbi finds the exact optimum among the candidates retained in the constructed lattice. Candidate construction, edge scoring and path search are separate stages: build alternatives cheaply, score compatible neighbors together, and search the resulting graph.

sections.title: From candidate lattices to coherent speculative drafts
paragraphs: Parallel speculative drafting creates a related setting: several candidates are available at each future position, but individually attractive choices need not form a useful draft. LiLiCorr keeps top-K candidates, computes incoming and outgoing vectors in a lightweight network, scores adjacent compatibility with batched operations, and performs a greedy walk. Its training objective targets accepted prefixes and co-adapts the drafter and scoring head.

The connection to Sequence-to-Lattice is the candidate–edge–path architecture. Translation candidates come from an alignment-based lookup model; LiLiCorr candidates come from a parallel drafter. Sequence-to-Lattice uses exact Viterbi for a complete path objective; LiLiCorr uses local normalization and greedy selection aligned with prefix acceptance.

DiffuSpec uses a diffusion model as a parallel drafter and introduces Causal-consistency Path Search over its token lattice, together with draft-length adaptation from acceptance feedback. Here the graph mediates between bidirectional draft proposals and an autoregressive verifier. A lattice describes the candidate organization; the scoring rule and verification procedure determine what selecting a path accomplishes.

sections.title: Choose the inference objective before choosing the graph
paragraphs: Three operations over the same graph answer different questions. Maximization finds the best complete path under a score. Marginalization sums over alternatives to measure probability or train a latent model. Sampling draws a sequence according to a distribution. Replacing one operation with another changes the algorithm even when the nodes and edges are identical.

A small numerical example makes the distinction concrete. Suppose the first decision offers A with probability 0.6 and B with probability 0.4. The strongest continuation after A has conditional probability 0.5; after B it has probability 0.9. Greedy selection begins with A. Whole-path maximization chooses B because 0.4 × 0.9 exceeds 0.6 × 0.5. In speculative decoding, the target verifier introduces another objective: the useful quantity is the accepted prefix, together with the cost of producing it.

To compare implementations, identify the candidate set, the edge dependence, the normalization, and the inference operation. Then measure the work that dominates runtime: neural passes, candidate scoring, dynamic programming, and verification.

sections.title: Run higher-order path search
paragraphs: Download the self-contained joint-decoding notebook or Python script. A three-token compatibility factor changes the sequence selected from a small candidate lattice. Max-sum dynamic programming finds the best path, and sum-product computes the global normalizer.

A separate locally normalized example demonstrates why greedy token selection and whole-path Viterbi search choose different paths. The examples expose exact structured inference on fixed scores. The papers supply the neural scoring, higher-order cascade, pruning and candidate-construction methods described above.
The code runs with Python 3.9+ and its standard library. Download all three examples and numerical checks.

title: Attention as a Latent Variable: Modeling a Distribution over Attention
description: Yuntian Deng and colleagues’ Latent Alignment and Variational Attention (NeurIPS 2018) models attention as a latent variable with output marginalization and learned posterior inference.
lead: Latent Alignment and Variational Attention, by Yuntian Deng, Yoon Kim, Justin Chiu, Demi Guo, and Alexander M. Rush, develops attention as an explicit latent variable with variational inference. First released on July 10, 2018 and published at NeurIPS 2018, it models a distribution over where a network attends and integrates predictions over that distribution. Categorical and Dirichlet alignments make this a general approach to modeling attention uncertainty.

sections.title: Normalized attention weights and a probabilistic model
paragraphs: An attention vector contains nonnegative weights that sum to one. That numerical property does not specify how uncertainty enters the prediction. A deterministic mechanism constructs one context vector from those weights and applies the downstream network once. A latent-variable mechanism defines alternative attention states, predicts under them, and integrates their contributions.

Write the attention state as z and the downstream computation as f. In general, f(E[z]) ≠ E[f(z)]. For a simple illustration, let z be 0 or 2 with equal probability and let f(z) = z². Applying f to the mean gives 1; averaging the two outputs gives 2. Neural prediction contains nonlinear operations, so moving the expectation across the network changes the model. This is the distinction between an average representation and an average over predictions.

sections.title: Marginalizing attention at the output
paragraphs: Let x include the observed input and the query, y be the output, and z be a categorical attention state. The latent model predicts p(y | x) = Σ_z p(z | x) p(y | x, z). Each attention state supplies an output distribution; its attention probability weights that distribution. A continuous attention state uses an integral in place of the sum.

During training, the observed answer y lets an inference network learn q(z | x, y), a posterior approximation used by the variational objective. At prediction time, the model combines outputs using p(z | x). For translation, the training inference network sees the source and target sentence; generation uses the source and the target prefix already produced.

sections.title: Latent alignment and variational attention
paragraphs: The 2018 paper makes alignment an explicit variable in the generative model. It studies categorical alignments, which select one source element, and Dirichlet alignments, which distribute attention across a mixture of elements. Amortized variational inference learns a posterior conditioned on observed inputs and outputs. Variance-reduction methods make latent inference practical, with experiments in machine translation and visual question answering.
Prior attention asks where to attend before the answer is known. Posterior attention asks which alignment explains an observed answer. These are different conditional distributions.

sections.title: What a posterior over attention tells you
paragraphs: Imagine an image containing two people and a question asking who is holding a cup. Before seeing the answer, the model assigns attention probability to both people. Once the answer is observed, posterior inference redistributes probability toward alignments that explain it.

The distinction also matters when attention is composed with another probabilistic component. Explicit variables expose which quantities are conditioned on, which alternatives are integrated out, and what an approximation replaces. A sampled attention vector, its expectation, and its most probable value answer different questions; naming the distribution makes those choices inspectable.

sections.title: How related attention methods differ
paragraphs: Show, Attend and Tell (ICML 2015) studies deterministic soft attention and sampled hard attention for image captioning. Its stochastic formulation uses a variational lower bound and a sampling-based learning rule. It provides an early reference for probabilistic selection; Latent Alignment and Variational Attention develops learned posterior inference for alignment and tighter variational training.

Structured Attention Networks (ICLR 2017) defines distributions over structured selections, including subsequences and syntactic trees. Differentiable graphical-model inference supplies expected annotations to the surrounding network. This enriches the structure of attention. Computing an expected annotation remains a separate operation from marginalizing the final nonlinear prediction over every attention structure.

Variational Attention for Sequence-to-Sequence Models (COLING 2018) models the context vector with Gaussian random variables in a variational encoder-decoder. Its purpose is to prevent deterministic attention from bypassing the model’s latent space. The latent object is the context vector, distinct from the categorical or simplex-valued alignment variable in Latent Alignment and Variational Attention.

Bayesian Attention Modules (NeurIPS 2020) constructs stochastic attention weights by normalizing Weibull or lognormal variables. Reparameterized training and data-dependent priors make the modules usable across attention architectures. This develops the broad distribution-over-attention perspective with a different distribution family and training construction.

sections.title: Four questions for a probabilistic attention model
paragraphs: Start with the random object: a selected position, a distribution over positions, a context vector, or an entire structured selection. Next specify the prior and the information available to the posterior. Then identify what the prediction integrates: an intermediate representation or the output likelihood. Finally state whether training and prediction enumerate states, sample them, use an expectation, or optimize a variational approximation.

Latent Alignment and Variational Attention uses categorical and simplex-valued alignments; Variational Attention for Sequence-to-Sequence Models uses Gaussian context vectors. The latent quantity and inference problem distinguish these two models.

sections.title: Run exact and variational attention
paragraphs: Download the self-contained attention notebook or Python script. It compares averaging source features before a nonlinear predictor with averaging output probabilities over categorical attention states.

The example computes the posterior for an observed label and optimizes a categorical variational distribution. The difference between exact log likelihood and the ELBO equals KL divergence to the exact posterior. It uses fixed generative parameters for one observation; the paper learns an amortized inference network across examples and also studies Dirichlet attention.
The code runs with Python 3.9+ and its standard library, without model weights, API keys or GPU resources. Download all three examples and numerical checks.

title: Evaluating generated text beyond fluency: story structure and entity consistency
description: Model Criticism for Long-Form Text Generation (Deng, Kuleshov and Rush, EMNLP 2022) evaluates discourse coherence, coreference and topicality through latent structure.
lead: Model Criticism for Long-Form Text Generation, by Yuntian Deng, Volodymyr Kuleshov, and Alexander M. Rush, evaluates the high-level structure of language-model output: how a document progresses, how it refers to entities, and how its topics relate. First released on October 16, 2022 and published at EMNLP 2022, it introduced a framework that maps real and generated text into latent structures and compares their distributions. This gives long-form text evaluation a structural test alongside word-level fluency.

sections.title: Separate fluent wording from coherent structure
paragraphs: A generated story reads: “Mira left the key at home. At the locked cabin, she opened the door with that key.” Both sentences are fluent; the story skips the event that makes the key available. An article presents another structural problem when it introduces a method, gives results, and then switches to an unrelated introduction. Evaluating these outputs requires stating the high-level property being tested.

Word-level perplexity measures how well a model predicts tokens. It does not directly measure section transitions, coreference structure, or topical relationships. The paper demonstrates this distinction with synthetic data whose generative process is known: strong next-token prediction coexists with a poor fit to the underlying latent transitions.

sections.title: Choose a critic that expresses the property being tested
paragraphs: The framework introduces a critic with a generative model of latent structure and observed text. Its posterior maps a document into a distribution over latent variables. Criticism then compares the structures inferred from generated samples with those inferred from reference data, using the same critic for both.

One diagnostic is the expected negative log probability of inferred latent variables under the critic’s prior. Aggregating it produces a latent cross-entropy, reported as latent perplexity in the experiments. This makes the measured property explicit: an evaluator of section order and an evaluator of entity reuse need different latent models. The critic supplies an assumption about structure; it is not the language model under evaluation.

sections.title: Three structural questions
paragraphs: Discourse coherence asks whether sections follow the transitions found in real documents. The experiments examine scientific articles and Wikipedia, including generation with and without explicit section-title cues. Coreference asks whether generated text reproduces the patterns of references to entities. Topicality asks whether topic relationships match reference documents.

These are distinct diagnoses. The paper finds that its transformer language models capture topical correlations while struggling with coherence and coreference. A single overall quality score would hide this difference.

sections.title: Entity consistency in generated stories
paragraphs: Consider “Nora gave Eli a key. She left. Eli opened the door.” An entity representation assigns the two mentions of Nora, “Nora” and “She,” to one entity, and the two mentions of Eli to another. It records which entity each expression refers to and where the mention occurs. This turns a passage into a sequence of entity references that can be compared across human-written and generated stories.

The paper’s coreference experiment extracts these mention patterns and scores their distribution with a critic, including patterns in which a pronoun lacks a local antecedent. Its discourse critic examines section transitions, and its topic critic examines topic relationships. An evaluation of the key’s location in the earlier story would specify event and object-state variables as the property to test.

sections.title: Relate model criticism to story metrics
paragraphs: OpenMEVA evaluates the evaluators. Its controlled perturbations test whether automatic metrics respond to errors in coherence and remain stable under meaning-preserving changes. Latent-space model criticism instead asks which structural distributions a generator has learned. The two approaches answer different experimental questions and fit together in an evaluation suite.

The story-evaluation survey by Dingyi Yang and Qin Jin organizes broader criteria such as coherence, character development, and interestingness. Human assessment or an LLM judge answers reader-facing questions; a specified structural critic supplies a reproducible diagnostic tied to a particular property.

sections.title: Design a long-form evaluation
paragraphs: Start with the failure you want to detect, then define its latent representation and reference corpus. Fit or specify the critic, check its behavior on real texts and known structural errors, and apply it identically to reference and generated samples. Keep generation conditions, document lengths, and sample counts visible so that the comparison answers the intended question.
Report word-level and structural measurements separately. The original paper and released code implement separate diagnostics for coherence, coreference, and topicality.

title: Diffusion rendering: LaTeX formulas and SMILES molecule images
description: Learned diffusion rendering turns supplied LaTeX code into formula images and SMILES strings into molecular drawings. Original ICLR 2023 work by Yuntian Deng, Noriyuki Kojima, and Alexander M. Rush.
lead: A diffusion model can learn to render a supplied LaTeX formula into a mathematical image, or a supplied SMILES string into a two-dimensional molecular structure image. Yuntian Deng, Noriyuki Kojima, and Alexander M. Rush introduced this approach in Markup-to-Image Diffusion Models with Scheduled Sampling, released on October 11, 2022 and published at ICLR 2023. Their learned renderer covers LaTeX mathematics, SMILES molecules, HTML table layouts, and LilyPond sheet music. Scheduled sampling trains the denoiser to correct errors in its own intermediate predictions.

sections.title: How does a diffusion model render a LaTeX formula?
paragraphs: The input is LaTeX source code and the output is an image of the specified formula. For example, \frac{a}{b} + c^2 describes a fraction followed by a squared term. A learned renderer must place the numerator above the denominator and position the superscript correctly. In this task, diffusion is the image-generation method; the formula supplied to it defines the mathematical content.

The model learns this mapping from paired markup and rendered images, including the formula pairs in im2latex-100k. At inference, it conditions a sequence of image-denoising steps on the supplied markup. The denoiser turns image noise into the rendered pixels, learning the relationship between source tokens, symbols, and layout.

The same input-to-image formulation applies to HTML table layouts and LilyPond music notation. These domains make the dependencies concrete: a table cell must occupy its specified row and column, and a note must have the pitch and duration described by the source.

sections.title: How does a SMILES string become a molecular drawing?
paragraphs: SMILES specifies the molecule through an atom-and-bond sequence. In SMILES-to-image rendering, that molecule is supplied as the input, and the diffusion model generates its two-dimensional structural drawing. For example, CC(=O)O specifies acetic acid; the drawing must preserve the stated atoms, single bonds, and carbon–oxygen double bond. This is a task-format example, with original model outputs available in the paper and code repository.

The molecular identity is fixed by the input SMILES. What the model learns is how to depict that structure in pixels. The Markup-to-Image experiments evaluate agreement with a reference drawing, connecting the generated image directly to the supplied symbolic description.

sections.title: A plausible image is not enough
paragraphs: These images demand exact symbolic fidelity. An extra minus sign changes a formula; an incorrect bond changes a molecule; a shifted note changes a score. An image that resembles the right domain still fails when its symbols do not match the input. Layout errors also propagate: an extra symbol displaces what follows.

The paper therefore evaluates alignment with the reference rendering. Its primary metric treats binarized images as sequences of columns and uses dynamic time warping, with tolerance for small shifts. Pixel error and additional image-similarity metrics provide complementary measurements. The paper explicitly distinguishes these criteria from natural-image scores that emphasize visual fidelity and broad semantics.

sections.title: Train the denoiser on its own intermediate states
paragraphs: Standard diffusion training constructs noisy inputs from ground-truth images. During sampling, the next denoising step instead receives the result of previous model predictions. Mistakes in those predictions change the states encountered later. The paper analyzes this mismatch as a sequential decision problem with compounding errors, connecting diffusion sampling to exposure bias.

Scheduled sampling changes the training inputs so that the denoiser encounters model-generated states and learns to correct its own errors. This adapts a principle previously studied in sequence generation to diffusion training. The experiments compare scheduled sampling with the baseline across all four rendering domains.

sections.title: Markup alignment and diffusion exposure bias
paragraphs: The rendering thread continues in FSA-CDM, by Guojin Zhong and colleagues, published at ACM Multimedia 2023. It evaluates the same four-domain task and adds fine-grained sequence alignment, contextual modeling, and contrastive training signals. Its contribution addresses how markup tokens correspond to visual structure, alongside the denoising process.

The diffusion-training thread connects to Input Perturbation Reduces Exposure Bias in Diffusion Models, published at ICML 2023. That method perturbs training inputs to simulate prediction errors. Both train the denoiser for the states it encounters during sampling: scheduled sampling uses model-generated inputs, while input perturbation adds synthetic errors.

sections.title: Inspect the original examples and implementation
paragraphs: The released repository includes side-by-side animations of scheduled sampling, the baseline, and ground truth for formulas, tables, music, and molecules. These examples expose the intermediate denoising trajectory.

For a new learned-rendering task, define paired source and target data, identify the symbolic errors that change meaning, and select metrics that expose them. The released resources include the original datasets, checkpoints, code, and recorded examples.

title: Interactive Training: human and LLM control of ongoing model training
description: Humans and LLM agents use live feedback to change learning rates and data or request checkpoints in an active job. Interactive Training introduced the framework at EMNLP 2025.
lead: Interactive Training lets a human or LLM agent read live training feedback and intervene in the same active neural-network training job. The controller changes optimizer settings or training data, or requests checkpoint operations, then observes the subsequent training behavior. Wentao Zhang, Yang Young Lu, and Yuntian Deng introduced the framework in Interactive Training: Feedback-Driven Neural Network Optimization, first released on October 2, 2025 and published at EMNLP 2025 System Demonstrations. Interactive Training 2, released on July 17, 2026, extends it with a reusable protocol for live control.
terms: LLM agent control of ongoing training

sections.title: What closes the loop between an LLM agent and a running training job?
paragraphs: The feedback is the state of training: loss curves, evaluation results, gradient norms, and the current settings. The action is an executable change to the running job. A human or LLM agent chooses an intervention from this feedback; the training process applies it and reports what happens next.

The model under training continues to learn through its optimizer. The external controller steers that optimization process by changing the controls exposed by the application. This gives “LLM training control” a concrete meaning: the agent observes and acts on the job that is already running.
items: Observe: read recent training metrics and the current configuration.
Decide: select a learning-rate, data, or checkpoint intervention using that feedback.
Apply: send the request through the control server to the training loop.
Observe again: inspect the applied action and the subsequent training measurements.

sections.title: How is the learning rate adjusted during training?
paragraphs: The 2025 paper demonstrates an LLM agent receiving training logs and changing the learning rate while optimization is underway. The decision uses the observed trajectory. A loss spike, gradient instability, or poor progress gives the controller evidence for its next action; the modified learning rate then affects subsequent optimizer steps.

Interactive Training also exposes gradient clipping, training-data changes, and checkpoint operations. Its original case studies cover human intervention, LLM-driven intervention, and real-time training-data updates. Together, these examples show how feedback-driven control extends beyond a learning-rate schedule to the ongoing training process.

sections.title: The 2025 system: monitoring connected to intervention
paragraphs: The original framework uses a control server to mediate between a human or automated agent and the training process. Its Trainer integration exposes commands for optimizer hyperparameters, data handling, and checkpoints. A live interface lets the controller observe training and submit changes instead of editing a static recipe and relaunching the program.

The paper presents three case studies spanning training stability, sensitivity to initial hyperparameters, and changing user needs. Its LLM-driven learning-rate example demonstrates an agent reading feedback and intervening during optimization. The system connects live observation and intervention to the training loop, while the optimizer continues updating model parameters.

sections.title: The 2026 extension: one protocol for different controllers
paragraphs: Interactive Training 2, by Wentao Zhang, Xuanhe Pan, Han Zhou, Yang Lu, and Yuntian Deng, replaces a fixed Trainer-specific command vocabulary with registered settings and actions. A TrainingSession exposes typed controls and descriptions. Humans, scripts, heuristics, and LLM agents submit requests through the same interface.

The training application chooses control points at which queued requests are validated and applied. An ordered journal connects requests to execution results, evaluations, checkpoints, and controller decisions. The Aim workspace brings this record together with live metrics. The paper also distinguishes within-round interventions from cross-round planning: a new round starts a fresh model and optimizer, while a textual journal carries observations and reflections forward.

sections.title: Compare mechanisms, controllers, and experiments
paragraphs: LiveTune predates Interactive Training and exposes LiveVariables for changing optimization parameters without restarting the loop. It supplies an earlier mechanism for live parameter adjustment. Interactive Training’s focus is the human and AI-agent workflow around training, and v2 makes the control vocabulary and event record reusable across applications.

AI Training Manager studies a bounded LLM supervisor that asynchronously reads telemetry and adjusts a running recipe. Its experiments introduce specific failure modes in supervised learning and reinforcement learning. Controller-level comparisons concern the evidence available to the agent, the actions it can request, and how later outcomes affect its decisions.

sections.title: Design an observable feedback loop
paragraphs: Expose controls that the training application can actually apply, and define when changes take effect. Record the observation that motivated a request, the requested value, the applied value, the step of application, and the subsequent measurements. A submitted request and a successful update are different events. Keeping them linked makes the behavior inspectable.

Evaluate an automated controller against a stated training objective under explicit workloads and budgets. Count its inference and intervention overhead, preserve the run history, and separate improvements within a continuing run from results of newly initialized rounds.
